comments.author: @King-wl6zj
comments.text:
A lot of this video’s arguments are pulled straight from Guns, Germs, and Steel. A geographic determinist take that modern historians and economists have widely discredited (despite a few fair points like desertification and naturual Barriers in the Deep South) 

1. Malaria and tsetse flies were real hurdles but as all are geographical hurdles anywhere (whether that be snow, being landlocked etc)  but Africans weren't passive victims… communities developed botanical pharmacology, genetic resistances (sickle cell and Duffy negative blood types) aswell as brush-clearing techniques to manage them. Even inside the tsetse belt, dense forest states thrived without ox plows (Benin, Asante and Kongo being obvious three) by using river canoe networks and farming crops. Ironically Africans independently developed farming (unlike Europeans, who imported farming). And Ironically, the Sahel had fewer tsetse flies yet remained less densely populated than the forest and southern regions for most of history.


2. Africa has always had centralized states and massive intra-continental and global trade networks across the Sahara, the Indian Ocean, and major rivers long before Atlantic ports mattered. Ethiopia was literally intergrated into the global trade system before most of Europe was and was at one point one of the four great powers of the world, the ancient Greeks literally saw border Europeans as barbaric and unintelligent, whereas they taught Aethopians (modern day east black Africans) as “blameless” intelligent and sophisticated(2,500-2,800 years ago) . The Mali Empire was also one of the richest empires in the Middle Ages (700 years ago) and controlled most of the world’s gold and salt supply and Benin was constantly praised by the Dutch as being larger than Lisbon, orderly and well governed. They also traded local goods first before the intensification of the Atlantic slave trade centuries later. (540 years ago) 


3. The biggest hole in the geography thesis is that Africa's historically wealthiest, most powerful regions (Mali, Ethiopia, Chad, Congo, Sudan) are among the poorest today, while historically smaller, less centralized regions (Botswana, Gabon, Kenya, Rwanda) are among the most developed. Geography didn't suddenly change in 1884. Thus this correlation is largely an empirical leap on the videos part. 
The truth is that colonialism, the transatlantic slave trade, and global trade imbalances are what structurally shaped African underdevelopment and it’s not even close.

comments.text: The tropics overall are a poorer region than the north and south temperate zones. The tropics usually have poorer soil compared to the temperate zones. There is also more competition for resources from other organisms, which harms agricultural output. The tropics are a more challenging place to build a strong diversified economy. Africa is the most tropical continent on Earth with around 80% of it's land within the tropics. Not surprisingly, the most developed areas in Africa have been in temperate North Africa and temperate South Africa. In this interglacial period, the middle latitudes reign supreme.
